item.title: Will Saddam Haftar be Libya’s next president?
item.description:
Will Saddam Haftar be Libya’s next president? Expert comment thilton.drupal 20 November 2026

The son of commander Khalifa Haftar has consolidated his position as heir apparent and expanded his influence. But his pursuit of the presidency could bring Libya back into conflict.

Saddam Haftar, the son of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF) commander Khalifa Haftar, has recently visited several foreign capitals in an apparent attempt to boost his international standing. This has been seen as part of a concerted push to become Libya’s next president.

This effort will define Libya’s politics for the coming months. It has huge implications for the country’s political future amid a US-led push for a national government that would unify Libya’s two rival administrations: the LAAF-controlled administration in eastern Libya and the Government of National Unity (GNU) in Tripoli. Strong opposition to Saddam’s goals in western Libya also means that the risk of conflict is increasing.

Saddam becomes heir apparent

For many years, there have been questions over Khalifa Haftar’s succession. The assumption has been that Haftar, 83, would remain in direct control of the LAAF while alive. It was speculated that the LAAF could fragment without Haftar, given the LAAF’s status as a hybrid of a military institution and a family enterprise.  

However, in recent years, Haftar has increasingly taken a back seat as his sons Saddam, Khaled, Belgassim and al-Sadiq have come to the fore. Their rise became clearer after the failure of the LAAF to capture Tripoli in 2020, which led Haftar to reassess his approach. Over subsequent years, the LAAF was restructured. Its forces were placed under the command of Saddam and Khaled, who gained responsibility for land forces and security units respectively. 

Meanwhile, Belgassim developed strong networks and influence in political circles. He was instrumental in the formation of a new government that sought to replace the sitting GNU in Tripoli. In 2023, Belgassim also assumed the helm of the Libyan Development and Reconstruction Programme, formed after floods killed several thousand people in Derna, which provided a new narrative of development for the Haftar family.

However, Khalifa’s appointment of Saddam as deputy general commander in August 2025 sealed his position as heir apparent. Saddam has become the most powerful of the sons through not just his military position, but also his alleged increasing influence via proxies over the oil and gas and banking sectors in eastern Libya.

The Boulos initiative

Saddam’s rise is important in the context of the push for a unified government in Libya. This has been led by Massad Boulos, the US Special Advisor for Africa and the Middle East. Under Boulos’ plan, a unified government would be formed as part of a deal between the two ruling families: the Haftars, who control eastern Libya, and the Dabaibas, who control the Tripoli-based GNU.

While the US has not publicized the parameters of the deal, insiders have said that Saddam Haftar would become a member of the Presidency Council, the three-person body whose chairman is Libya’s de facto head of state. The Dabaiba family would retain the prime minister’s post.

Related work

Why US plans for power-sharing in Libya will not work

Negotiating processes had previously focused on seeking agreement between Libya’s fractious institutions: the chronically divided House of Representatives in eastern Libya and the Tripoli-based High State Council. But the US plan has broken with this formula, instead seeking agreement between the Haftars and the Dabaibas. The first agreement made through this channel was a deal on budgetary spending in April 2026.

Subsequently, the United Nations adapted to the new format. The UN Mission’s ‘4+4’ committee brought together a combination of representatives from the GNU, LAAF, the House of Representatives and the High State Council. The 4+4 reached agreement on a roadmap for national elections in August.

This pivot towards negotiations being between the LAAF and the GNU – essentially between the emissaries of Saddam Haftar and the Dabaibas – is more significant than the content of the agreement. It officially places Saddam’s LAAF General Command as a negotiating party with parity with the internationally recognized GNU.  

Path to the presidency?

Buoyed by these diplomatic advances, Saddam has recently made significant moves to expand his influence.

The ousting of the longtime speaker of the House of Representatives in October – and his replacement with a figure known for his support for the LAAF – is widely understood to have been orchestrated by Saddam.

Shortly after, the House of Representatives moved to ratify a controversial memorandum of understanding with Turkey over the recognition of drilling rights in the eastern Mediterranean. Insiders have said privately that Saddam pushed for this move, which angered Egypt and European countries, presumably with the aim of securing Ankara’s support for his push for the presidency in return.

Then, on 26 October, the governor of the Central Bank of Libya was replaced, reportedly due to a private agreement between the Haftars and the Dabaibas. The Central Bank holds a critical place in the management of Libya’s economy, overseeing the distribution of foreign currency and dinar payments that are so crucial to Libya’s leaders.

That same week, Saddam was in Turkey for talks with the GNU on military reunification.

Alongside strengthening his influence over important institutions in Libya, Saddam has consequently emerged as the apparent partner of preference for the some of the most influential international actors. He is seen as someone who can get things done and maintain order in comparison to the messy picture of contested power in western Libya.

The enduring Haftar ‘problem’ and the risk of conflict

Saddam is now central to any political effort to reunify the country. His ambitions to enter Tripoli are widely known. Those familiar with the security sector in the capital note that local allies of Saddam are seeking to prepare the ground for his arrival.

But opposition to – and mistrust of – Saddam in western Libya remains strong, especially in key constituencies such as the city of Misrata. This has not been helped by the uncovering of a sleeper cell, allegedly linked to the LAAF, that was accused of seeking to cause damage to oil and gas infrastructure in the city of Zawiya in August.

Many doubt that Saddam is willing to share power. It therefore seems no meaningful guarantees can be provided to Saddam’s opponents to reassure them. Western Libyan actors would like to separate the discussion of military reunification from political reunification as a result.

Consequently, while the Dabaiba family may be willing to cut deals to retain a modus vivendi with Saddam, it is highly unlikely to sign a deal making Saddam president. This is evident in the fact that no deal has yet been reached, despite intensive efforts over months by Boulos.

This, in turn, creates a problem. It is not clear how Saddam’s rapid rise and apparent aspirations for president can be squared with his opponents’ steadfast opposition to him. And they are unlikely to go anywhere, considering that the Dabaibas are entrenched in power too.

This fundamental difference runs deeper than the Boulos initiative. As one source in the security sector told me: even if there were elections, Saddam would not accept the results if he loses, and his opponents would not accept the results if he wins.

If Saddam continues to push for the presidency, Libya therefore faces a heightened risk of conflict. Many of his opponents would seemingly prefer the messy situation in Tripoli to prevail over a new order that could ultimately end up squarely under Saddam’s control. But, given the strength of international support building behind Saddam’s campaign, their options are narrowing.

item.title: The ICJ’s Myanmar finding shifts the dial – a little – on the grounds for a guilty verdict in a genocide case
item.description:
The ICJ’s Myanmar finding shifts the dial – a little – on the grounds for a guilty verdict in a genocide case Expert comment jon.wallace 20 November 2026

The Court’s unusually split decision seems to adjust how intent to destroy a group ‘in whole or in part’ is established.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the highest court in the world, has ruled that Myanmar is guilty of genocide. According to the Court, the ‘clearance’ campaign by the Myanmar military against its Rohingya minority of 2017 was aimed at the destruction, in whole or in part, of that community. The finding in this case, which was brought before the Court by the Gambia in 2019, will reverberate far beyond Myanmar and its immediate environment.

The ICJ’s previous genocide cases

The Rohingya are a mainly Muslim ethnic group that has been excluded from Myanmar citizenship and discriminated against for decades. In the wake of attacks by terrorist groups against the military in 2016, some 10,000 Rohingya were killed, and over 85 per cent of its population of around 850,000 were displaced from Myanmar over the following year in a campaign of killings, rape and the burning of villages.

Hear directly from the experts

Get nuanced insights from Chatham House experts on the issues shaping the global policy and geopolitical landscape.

The ICJ has established a very high bar for confirming that genocide has occurred. Several cases, including those brought by Croatia against Serbia and Sudan against the UAE, have been unsuccessful. 

Others are still ongoing, addressing the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda, Ukraine and the Russian Federation, and Gaza.

Only once before, in relation to the 1995 Srebrenica massacre of 8,000 men and boys in Bosnia and Herzegovina, has the ICJ confirmed genocide. But controversially, it failed to attribute the atrocity to its alleged author, the Republic of Serbia (then the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia) under Slobodan Milosevic.

This new decision of the Court moves the dial ever so slightly, reducing the legal hurdles on the way towards a finding of genocide. 

The grounds for a finding of genocide

According to the Genocide Convention of 1948, genocide requires three elements. 

First, it must be directed against a protected group, defined by national, ethnic, racial or religious characteristics. Second, there must be prohibited acts directed against members of the group. This includes killings, causing serious bodily or mental harm, inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about the destruction of the group, or measures intended to prevent births or forcibly transferring children to another group. 

But critically, even if a pattern of such practices is clearly evident, this must be carried by the specific intent to destroy the group as such ‘in whole or in part’ – the third element.

This may seem odd. If the result is the destruction of the group, one might argue that this should suffice to constitute genocide. Such conduct would clearly amount to a crime against humanity and other severe violations of human rights and humanitarian law. However, in defining what is sometimes called ‘the crime of crimes,’ the Genocide Convention imposes this additional criterion of specific intent. 

Of course, that is difficult to prove. States no longer record their decision to commit genocide in a formal document, as Hitler’s government did in the famous 1942 Wannsee Protocol, which planned the complete destruction of Europe’s Jewish population. 

Without such formal documentation, proof of the intent to destroy a group in whole or in part must be inferred from the nature of a systematic campaign of killing and other acts proscribed by the Genocide Convention that are directed at a defined population segment.

Previously, the Court asserted that such an inference can only be made if this pattern cannot be explained by any reason other than the intention to commit genocide. 

In its defence, Myanmar offered several alternative grounds to explain the nature of its armed campaign. It referred to the need to mount a counter-terrorism effort following attacks by rebel movements in Rakhine province, where most Rohingya used to reside. However, in view of the Court, this motivation would not explain the pattern of brutal attacks against the civilian population.

The Court also considered whether Myanmar’s conduct might simply have been directed at the forcible displacement of the Rohingya, rather than their destruction in whole or in part. This alone would be a serious international crime, but it would not quite amount to genocide.

However, the Court looked at the overall context of the long-standing campaign against the Rohingya – including discrimination, hate speech, the nature of the military operation and other culpable acts systematically targeting this group and affecting its ‘foundations’ or existence.

In broadening this overall context, and relying on the totality of the evidence, rather than just the well attested reports of individual atrocities, the Court was able to assert that the intent to commit genocide was the only reasonable inference that could be drawn.

The effect on other cases

This outcome will concern some governments involved in other ongoing cases regarding genocide. 

Ukraine brought a case before the ICJ in 2022, asking the Court to confirm that it had not committed genocide against Russian-speakers on its territory – a central claim made by Russia to justify its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that year. 

In another case, the DRC is alleging that Rwanda is involved in genocide conducted on its territory. In a further action, Nicaragua is alleging that Germany shares responsibility for the alleged genocide in Gaza due to its supply of arms to Israel. 

The Court’s Myanmar judgement may impact these cases. But international attention is mainly focused on the case’s implications for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel. 

In an initial, provisional phase of the case, the Court found that there may be a plausible case of genocide in relation to Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.

Counsel for Israel and South Africa, along with the over 20 others states that have intervened in that case, will now assess the Court’s finding and ask: what would the outcome be if the matrix of factors applied by the ICJ in the Myanmar case were applied to Israel’s armed campaign in Gaza? Would this exercise demonstrate that the intent to commit genocide is the only reasonable explanation for the character of that campaign?

Related work

South Africa’s genocide case against Israel: The International Court of Justice explained

The key clauses in the Myanmar judgement were adopted by an unusually divided Court, by a majority of 9 to 6. The ICJ decides according to the applicable law, not the politics involved in a given situation. But its decision will probably be criticized by some as having lowered the threshold for the identification of genocide, perhaps with a view to confirming the relevance of the Court and of the international rule of law. International law has been largely disregarded in many recent conflicts – especially its humanitarian provisions. 

On the other hand, those opposing the Court’s finding might be accused of trying to prevent a precedent being established when it comes to evaluating the Gaza case.

In addition to political controversy, the case raises another important issue: A third state, The Gambia – which is not involved in Myanmar’s conflict – managed to obtain a ruling in favour of a dispossessed and internationally disenfranchised minority group located a continent away. 

The Gambia brought the action with the support of the Organization of the Islamic Conference and senior international lawyers, adopting a kind of international public service role in defence of the international public order. It confirmed that all states have a firm legal interest in compliance with that rule by all other states, and that parties to the Genocide Convention can bring a case to the Court in defence of the prohibition of genocide. 

The Court even considered that in this case between The Gambia and Myanmar, it has the authority to rule on the entitlement of the Rohingya as the ultimate beneficiaries of the obligation to prevent genocide to restitution and compensation from their own government. In this way, it has reasserted and indeed extended its role of guardian of the international rule of law at a time of challenge to global order.

North Korea Is Outsourcing Its Cybercrime Empire: Here’s How
item.description:
The software developer on the video call seemingly checks every box. He has a real face, a steady internet connection and a polished answer to every technical question. In reality though, he could be an Iranian or a South African developer who is being paid a few hundred dollars a month to play the part.

Once a U.S. company sends an offer letter and a work laptop, he steps aside. A North Korean operative, often working from China or Russia, logs in under the same name, does the job, sends the salary back to Pyongyang and quietly gains a foothold inside the company’s systems.

This is the newest twist in North Korea’s fake IT worker scheme. According to U.S. authorities, the state-run operation slips regime workers into remote tech jobs at Western companies under stolen or invented identities. The practice is growing as the regime’s hackers pull off the biggest thefts in cryptocurrency history, and the two efforts are more closely tied than most employers realize.

On Oct. 31, the FBI attributed the theft of more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, the world’s largest exchange, to the North Korean hacking cluster known as TraderTraitor. The Oct. 29 heist, the largest on record, is roughly three times what North Korean-linked hackers stole in all of 2025. Binance has since said the breach started with a job interview, in which attackers posing as recruiters had one of its engineers download a coding “assignment” laced with malware onto his work computer.

If a single fake job interview could open the door to the largest crypto theft on record, what can a North Korean operative do once a company actually hires him?

The hiring side of Pyongyang’s cyber operation is moving just as fast. Material Security counted 2,429 suspected North Korean job seekers in the hiring pipelines it monitored over the past year, and reported that 27 of them made it to the onboarding phase of the hiring process. At one company where a persona was onboarded just last month, roughly 277,000 files containing Social Security numbers were made available company-wide or through public links. CrowdStrike, a cybersecurity firm that tracks state-backed hacking groups, says it uncovers one or two suspected North Korean IT worker cases every day.

Increasingly, the scheme runs on hired help from third countries. Recruits in Iran, Syria, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia and South Africa have been paid to pose as job applicants on camera, according to American officials and private researchers.

The stakes reach well beyond payroll fraud.

A United Nations panel of experts reported in 2024 that malicious cyber activity generates about half of North Korea’s foreign currency income and according to one member state, funds some 40 percent of its weapons of mass destruction programs. CrowdStrike has linked the IT worker campaign to North Korea’s Munitions Industry Department, which runs its weapons production. Once inside a company, those workers can reach source code, customer data and internal networks.

“The money matters because it funds the weapons program, but I think the access is the bigger concern,” Jason Vest, chief technology officer of Binary Defense, tells The Cipher Brief. “These are bad actors sitting inside U.S. networks with legitimate credentials, and North Korea can decide at any point that stealing data or crypto is worth more than the paycheck.”

So how does it all really work behind the scenes, and what is Pyongyang trying to achieve?

A $500-a-Month Face for the Camera

Experts believe the scheme draws on a workforce that North Korea has spent decades building. South Korea’s spy agency estimated in 2024 that the North’s cyber operations employ about 8,400 people. According to a recent Reuters investigation, children as young as 11-years-old are selected for computer science training. The best go to military cyber units and those who don’t make the cut are trained to build software for Western firms through remote work.

Those operatives, mostly based in China, Russia and Southeast Asia, build fake Western personas with polished LinkedIn profiles and GitHub histories. They apply for remote jobs by the thousands. Then they send someone else to the interview.

Internal documents obtained by the threat intelligence firm Flare show how the recruiting works. One North Korean facilitator, known as “Sea,” wrote “Targeting Iran guys” in a spreadsheet tracking recruits. Another, “Eugene,” noted he was “Hiring new guys in Iran, Syria and SA.” Flare identified at least 14 Iranians in the pipeline since 2024, and at least two reportedly received offer letters from American employers.

Recruits were offered about $500 a month in cryptocurrency to work part-time as “interview associates,” with pay climbing to as much as $5,000 a month once a job was secured. Each stand-in was assigned a made-up American persona, such as “Jack Long,” a fake C#/.NET developer. When a stand-in failed an interview, the facilitator reviewed the recording and coached him for the next one.

The goal is straightforward. Every stand-in who clears an interview opens a job for a North Korean operator, and every job brings a paycheck for the regime and a login that gains access inside an American company. Flare’s documents show facilitators chasing blockchain jobs, onboarding at an American credit union and closing in on a position at one of the largest defense contractors in the United States.

The stand-ins are found the way any freelancer is. Kudelski Security, a Swiss firm, described developers in Iran, Syria and South Africa as ordinary citizens who accepted offers on LinkedIn. Flare researchers found that one recruiter’s pitch asked outright whether candidates were comfortable working under someone else’s identity, while dangling crypto payments that sidestep Iran’s banking embargo. Recruits knew they were lending their faces to someone else’s résumé, though the documents don’t show that all of them knew the someone else was North Korea.

For Pyongyang, who sits in front of the camera matters far less than what happens after the call. Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations and comparative politics at the University of Sydney, says North Korean sanctions evasion has long relied on third-country partners acting as the regime’s interface with the outside world.

“The North Koreans themselves aren’t in peril, and the third-party cut-outs are disposable from their perspective. The North Koreans want the money, and the access — who actually meets with the company is less important to them,” Hastings tells The Cipher Brief.

In other words, when a stand-in is caught, the Iranian or South African faces the consequences. The North Korean behind him recruits another face.

Why Sanctions Keep Missing the Mark

The move to foreign stand-ins is partly a result of Western success. Companies learned to catch North Koreans using AI face filters when they asked candidates to wave a hand in front of the camera or to insult North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on the spot. It seems a real person from Tehran or Johannesburg passes those tests easily.

“Just about every criminal scheme in history has adapted to bypass controls intended to stop it,” Alex Hamerstone, advisory solutions director at TrustedSec, tells The Cipher Brief.

Vest describes it as an evolution of the threat.

“Companies have gotten better at spotting deepfakes and camera tricks during video interviews, so North Korea started paying real people to take the interview for them,” he says. “Once the stand-in gets the job, a North Korean operator does the actual work.”

Washington has thrown indictments, raids and sanctions at the problem, with limited effect. On Oct. 14, the Justice Department announced charges against 14 people after FBI agents raided more than 40 suspected “laptop farms” in Texas, homes where facilitators keep company-issued computers so operatives overseas can appear to be working from the United States.

Prosecutors say the devices helped put North Korean workers inside more than 70 American companies. The Treasury Department has sanctioned facilitators from Vietnam to Spain, and a later round on Oct. 28 hit Russians accused of cashing out crypto for the network.

Each designation, however, catches a front company or an intermediary, and new ones replace them. Treasury estimates the IT worker program brought in nearly $800 million in 2024. The security firm DTEX traced about $1.97 million in worker payments through Korea Ryonbong General Corporation, a sanctioned defense company, and found that money moving through the network helps fund Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Hamerstone underscores that North Korea is already so isolated that additional sanctions are unlikely to have much effect, and prosecutions run into a numbers problem.

“If the quantity of individuals available to perpetrate a crime far exceeds the number who are caught and punished, the indictments are unlikely to have a significant effect on the proliferation of the activity,” he explains.

Vest sees the same gap from the defender’s side.

“Sanctions don’t do much against a country that’s already cut off, and the people getting indicted are never going to see a U.S. courtroom,” he explains. “The place this can be stopped is the hiring process at American companies, and right now it’s still too easy to get through.”

From Paycheck to Heist

It isn’t only corporate payrolls. On July 28, Todd Hemmen, a deputy assistant director in the FBI’s Cyber Capabilities Branch, told a Washington conference that agents had identified a North Korean remote IT worker on a federal job the week before. He did not say which agency. People who follow federal hiring suspect a contractor, since direct government jobs come with background checks. Contract IT support work rarely gets that level of vetting, and it can still come with a login to government networks.

Defense work is a prime target. In one case, a worker using a stolen American identity spent more than two months inside a California defense contractor’s systems, downloading export-controlled technical data. When workers get inside particularly valuable targets, CrowdStrike says it has seen that access handed to North Korean malware teams to collect intelligence. And when workers are exposed and fired, the FBI warns, some hold stolen source code and data for ransom.

Crypto companies sit at the center of the overlap. Chainalysis has found that North Korea pulls off its outsized heists by embedding IT workers inside crypto services to gain privileged access. In April, the trading platform Drift Protocol lost about $285 million in an operation it tied to a North Korean state-affiliated group, and said the people who met its team face to face were not North Korean nationals. Binance shows the reverse side of the same hiring channel, with North Korean hackers posing as the recruiters.

Hastings notes that the regime’s motives line up with its other revenue operations.

“As with everything related to North Korea’s money-making schemes, they want to make money, and the opportunity for espionage and information gathering is a bonus,” he stresses.

Hamerstone argues the distinction matters less than it seems.

“I don’t believe it is one or the other,” he observes. “Reports show that a significant portion of North Korea’s money comes from these types of activities, and if the assumption that North Korea having resources is a problem, then anything that provides additional funding to them is an issue.”

What Hiring Managers Keep Missing

Flare concluded “with high confidence” that North Korean operatives are deliberately targeting American defense contractors, cryptocurrency exchanges and financial institutions, where a single insider can do the most damage. In 2024, the security firm KnowBe4 says it caught a newly hired North Korean worker loading malware onto his company-issued Mac within minutes of receiving it.

The red flags tend to show up after the offer letter goes out. A new hire’s video stops working, or he asks for the company laptop to be shipped to an address that doesn’t match his résumé, or his payroll account changes a few weeks into the job. Network logs often trace his logins to a commercial VPN, and one company came up so often that the fraud-detection firm Spur published a free list of the service’s IP addresses so employers could screen for it.

At many companies, though, no single person is watching for any of this. HR runs the hiring and security runs the network, so the two sets of warning signs rarely end up in the same place.

Hamerstone points out that no single missing control is to blame.

“Employee vetting is not as strong and thorough as it should be, especially for remote roles with access to organizational resources,” he notes. “This ends up becoming even more of an issue because many organizations have weak access control within the organization, limited monitoring of employee access, and other missing foundational security controls.”

The FBI’s advice is old-fashioned: verify identity in person where possible and hold part of onboarding face to face. Third-country stand-ins make that harder. The person who shows up to an in-person meeting may be real and still may not be the person doing the work.

For Vest, the problem starts with how companies think about identity.

“They verify identity once, during the interview, and assume the person who shows up to work is the same one,” he adds. “Check again at onboarding, only ship laptops to verified addresses, and pay attention when a new hire is running remote access tools or logging in from somewhere that doesn’t match.”

item.title: Why the Houthis are always winning
item.description:
Saudi Arabia has fired the military commander leading its renewed offensive against Houthi rebels in Yemen.

It happened after Saudi-backed forces pulled back from an advance aimed at reclaiming territory along the Red Sea coast, including the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.

The country’s Saudi-backed government, which operates from its interim capital in Aden, launched this latest military offensive more than a month ago, in an attempt to drive out the Houthis and reclaim the capital, Sanaa.


Despite overwhelming aerial military superiority, and the renewed threat of a wider ground war, the Saudi military campaign already faces tactical setbacks. Riyadh has been here before, having waged a seven-year aerial bombing campaign that achieved nothing strategically.

But it did create and inflame one of the world’s worst humanitarian disasters. Those failed efforts also boosted the Houthis narrative as "defending the country" from Saudi aggression, despite that group's own targeting of aid groups and civilians.

The latest ramp up of war, and the aggressive Houthi response, just threatens to target and choke a civilian population already suffering from more than a decade of misery.

With no vital U.S. interest at stake, why would it militarily get involved in this disaster?

item.title: Europe should fund Ukraine’s defence industry as a partner, not a supplier
item.description:
Europe should fund Ukraine’s defence industry as a partner, not a supplier Expert comment jon.wallace 23 November 2026

Ukraine’s strikes on the Kerch Bridge and Russian navy show the extent of its defence industry’s abilities. The EU 2027 finance package should seek to boost that industry towards a lasting partnership.

In mid-November, Ukrainian forces destroyed a road span of the Kerch Bridge, linking occupied Crimea to mainland Russia. The strike used jet-powered drones and cruise missiles reportedly guided through an airborne relay network rather than Starlink. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the bridge strike as the seventh phase of an operation that had first targeted the air-defence, radar and electronic warfare systems protecting the crossing. 

Sequencing of that kind, combining several weapon types using communications under Ukrainian control, owes much to Ukrainian military planning. But the weapons and the relay network themselves reflect a Ukrainian defence sector that has learned to design, field and adapt systems in months, rather than the years typical of European procurement. 
The strike package was not wholly Ukrainian: Destinus, a Dutch-headquartered company, says its systems were the only foreign-made weapons used. Russia’s embassy in The Hague responded by asking publicly whether the Netherlands had joined the war. 

Days later, on 22 November, Kyiv said seven Ukrainian-made sea drones had successfully sunk the Russian corvette Merkury at the Benghazi Naval base in Libya. Unlike Kerch, this attack appears to have involved no foreign weapons, showing the kind of low-cost maritime capability Ukraine has developed and can exercise at range.

Ukraine’s innovation advantage

Ukraine’s defence industry has developed under conditions that no European procurement system faces. Weapons and systems are tested in an active warzone, providing immediate operational feedback and demanding compressed procurement cycles. Its production capacity has grown from around $1 billion in 2022 to an estimated $35 billion in 2025. EU member states together spent €418 billion on defence that year, so Ukraine’s edge is the speed of its innovation. 

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

The tempting conclusion is that a country able to produce such technology under these pressures can build anything Europe needs, including air defence, if the money is there. Indeed, Kyiv has called on partners to help build ‘the arsenal of the free world’ with Ukraine. However, operational effectiveness should not be confused with industrial capacity. 

Know-how is not the main constraint: Ukraine inherited much of the Soviet Union’s missile-design base, and its companies are now developing ballistic and anti-ballistic missiles alongside unmanned systems. 

The binding constraints are instead access to capital, production capacity, industrial facilities that are vulnerable to Russian attacks, and the availability of specialist components, particularly advanced electronics and seekers.

Of these, finance is the most immediate concern. The head of Ukraine’s Council of Defence Industry has said that manufacturers are operating at around 40 per cent of their potential capacity because the government is not placing enough orders. That suggests that additional funding could quickly unlock production potential. 

However, Europe’s requirements go beyond volume. Advanced air defence, particularly against ballistic missiles, depends on complex radar and sensor networks, high-end interceptors and industrial supply chains that require substantial investment and sustained development. Ukraine’s experience can inform European capability development. But it does not remove the need for Europe to build and maintain such capabilities itself.

The limits of a supplier relationship

There are other limitations on purchasing from Ukraine. Kyiv’s export framework is designed to protect its own forces. Companies may export only if they can also fulfil Ukrainian government contracts. Exports carry no intellectual property rights. And re-export requires Kyiv’s approval and attracts a 20 per cent tax.  

Even the drones built at the first Ukrainian joint venture in Germany are currently allocated to Ukraine’s armed forces. These are rational choices for a country fighting for its survival. But they mean that in a crisis, European governments could not assume Ukrainian output would be available for their own requirements, at least until Kyiv’s rules adapted.

A ceasefire would raise a different problem extending beyond supply-chain security. Ukraine’s advantage is tied to the operational environment in which its firms develop and test equipment. A settlement would necessarily reduce the operational feedback, procurement incentives and pressure that drive innovation. European planning should not assume that the wartime model will persist, or that Ukraine’s production priorities will stay aligned with Europe’s.

Closer cooperation also carries political risk: Moscow’s reaction to Destinus fits a pattern of embassy statements labelling Dutch support for Ukraine as participation in the conflict. European governments should anticipate diplomatic coercion and hostile activity directed against facilities, personnel and supply chains associated with Ukrainian defence production. Russia has already named European firms producing drones for Ukraine as potential targets. In August, an explosive-laden drone was found beside a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport, an attack Germany has since attributed to Russia. Such hybrid attacks could make some European governments more cautious about hosting joint production, underlining the importance of protecting facilities, personnel and supply chains.

From procurement to partnership

The European Commission’s proposed €45 billion loan to Ukraine for 2027, the second half of the EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, including €31.7 billion for defence, provides an opportunity to shape cooperation. The allocation of these funds will have long-term consequences beyond Ukraine’s immediate military requirements. 

Funding can support Ukrainian production for domestic use, establish joint ventures on European territory, or, where EU rules allow a derogation, finance procurement from established suppliers outside Europe, including the United States. 

Buying Ukrainian output sustains Ukraine’s defence. And buying from outside Europe fills immediate gaps. But only joint ventures build enduring capacity across Europe. Ukraine’s immediate needs, particularly for air defence this winter, must remain central to European assistance. But joint ventures are where support and European industrial development can converge, and where a meaningful share of the package should be directed.

The partnership should rest on a division of labour that draws on what Ukraine’s circumstances have produced. The war has given Ukraine’s defence industry what European nations cannot match during peacetime: urgency, a tolerance for failure, and feedback loops that are measured in days. 

Reinforced by Kyiv stripping out procurement, testing and regulatory barriers, Ukraine’s industry benefits from low-cost mass production and rapid iteration under pressure. That has delivered interceptor drones and long-range strike at a pace and cost that European procurement has, to date, struggled to match. 

Partnership offers the rest of Europe a way to learn from Ukraine’s experience of rapid development and operational feedback, while reinforcing the need to reform Europe’s procurement systems. Ukraine is already offering foreign firms the chance to test equipment in near-combat conditions alongside frontline units, through its state-backed Brave1 defence-tech cluster, and to pair with Ukrainian manufacturers for co-production. European states should take up that offer as partners rather than customers. 

European states and companies, in turn, bring radar and sensor technology, high-end interceptors, sovereign space-based communications, capital, and production sites beyond the reach of Russian missiles. 

Joint ventures and licensed production can bring these together, but only if they involve genuine technology transfer, shared research, integrated supply chains, and appropriate allocation priority when the future security picture shifts. Ukrainian reporting has described the German joint venture as closer to a showcase than the start of a systematic process, whereas Destinus reports output approaching 300 Ruta missiles a month.

Moving from individual projects to an enduring framework will require predictable multi-year financing and agreements on intellectual property that give Ukrainian and European manufacturers the confidence to invest together.

European leaders should therefore ask not only how much to spend on Ukraine, but how that spending can future-proof collective European security and capability. Treating Ukraine as a source of weapons risks creating a dependency that becomes visible only when European security is next under pressure. Building shared industrial capacity would strengthen Ukraine’s defence and Europe’s resilience at the same time.

For the first time a state, Myanmar, has been found directly responsible for the crime of genocide. item.title: Europe still isn’t ready for grey zone warfare
item.description:
Europe still isn’t ready for grey zone warfare Expert comment thilton.drupal 24 November 2026

As Russia and Iran intensify their grey zone attacks across the UK and Europe, national governments must improve their defences. They should begin by improving how they identify the perpetrators and communicate the dangers to the public.

Spoiled food and fires in France, a botched drone attack at Leipzig Airport in Germany and flights grounded by bomb threats in the UK and across the continent are only some of the recent grey zone attacks to hit Europe. 

As Europe’s adversaries – primarily Russia and Iran – increase the intensity and frequency of their grey zone attacks, national governments have been cautious and disjointed in their response. Governments need a stronger, collective response to avoid dangerous escalation.

Not quite war, not quite peace

The UK Ministry of Defence defines grey zone, or ‘sub-threshold,’ attacks as those which do not usually meet the legal definition of an act of war. Election interference, disinformation campaigns, cyberattacks, sabotage, harassment from drones, and manufactured security hoaxes all fall within this category.

Recently, Russia and Iran have presented the most significant state-based grey zone threats to Europe. Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, European states have fallen victim to an increasing number of grey zone attacks from Russia. Iran significantly intensified its grey zone efforts in Europe after the US and Israel launched strikes against it in late February 2026. China and North Korea, in addition to non-state actors like cybercrime syndicates, have also been previously accused of engaging in grey zone tactics across Europe.

Related work

The resilience gap: Are Europe’s societies ready for the next crisis?

The appeal of grey zone warfare lies in the ability of perpetrators to sow confusion and disunity among targeted populations and trigger failure in critical infrastructure systems, with the aim of gaining a strategic advantage without having to engage in full-blown armed conflict. Myriad grey zone attacks can strain governments’ resources, divide public opinion and distract attention. Internationally, they can also weaken cooperation towards shared objectives. 

European governments see Russia’s grey zone attacks as aimed at hampering their support and assistance for Ukraine. Russia is also likely testing European NATO allies’ capacity to absorb grey zone aggression without triggering its Article 5 mutual defence provisions. Tehran likely aims to disincentivise Europe from aligning with US and Israeli foreign policy objectives in the Middle East and is less likely than Russia to intend these attacks to be the instigation of outright conflict. 

Treading too lightly

To date, European national governments have struggled to effectively respond to grey zone activity in a way that deters future attacks. 

The nature of grey zone tactics inherently complicates the ability of European governments to respond or retaliate. They usually fall short of explicit acts of war, are difficult to immediately attribute to perpetrators, and mimic natural disruptions. 

European governments do not want grey zone attacks to lead to outright direct war with Russia or Iran, but this does not mean that they are not responding to these attacks. 

For example, Estonia has already publicly initiated court proceedings against Russian saboteurs who allegedly attempted to commit arson against a UAV manufacturer on 14 November. France has named Iran’s Revolutionary Guards as responsible for the October 2026 supermarket refrigerator hacks.

Germany, too, was quick to identify Russia for conducting the failed Leipzig Airport bomb attack in August 2026, acknowledging in a statement that the attack was part of ‘hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine’. In the same statement, the government affirmed the likelihood of similar attacks in the future while insisting that Germany is ‘not at war.’ Similarly, the commander of the UK’s Cyber and Specialist Operations Command recently stated that the UK is not ‘at war, but we’re not at peace either.’ 

European countries have responded to attacks by seemingly accepting that they will be a constant target of grey zone warfare, but they have generally failed to translate these warnings into a wider public awareness of the escalatory potential of these attacks. 

Attribution of recent attacks is helpful in establishing blame, but without wider public awareness of Russian, Iranian, and other sustained grey zone campaigns across the continent, there is a risk that the public misunderstands these attacks as one-off incidents. 

Europe should acknowledge that it is effectively under coordinated attack and communicate this publicly. Without securing public support for strengthened resilience measures, especially around critical infrastructure, Europe will remain limited to responses that are clandestine, reactive, and disjointed. 

Protecting infrastructure

The UK and other European governments must find ways to enhance security measures around critical infrastructure, given the increasing frequency with which it is being targeted. To respond more effectively, governments first need to take more preventive steps to protect their most obvious vulnerabilities to grey zone attacks.

Poland’s army, for example, was tasked in December 2025 to protect key energy infrastructure. Shortly after the freezer hacks in Europe, the UK’s proactive identification of a cybersecurity flaw enabled a cross-sector awareness campaign that prevented a similar hack occurring. 

Related work

After the RAF Fairford incident, the UK should develop its homeland defence forces

These kinds of measures signal a deeper readiness within national governments to deter grey zone attacks, though they are not without their costs: for example, dedicating military forces to protect infrastructure could impede frontline readiness. 

It is also harder for Western European countries to secure the domestic political will required for proactive defence than countries in Eastern Europe that are closer to Russia. In Western Europe, governments are less likely to feel confident to take drastic measures that could be interpreted domestically as initiating unnecessary conflict or increasing defence spending amid rising concerns over the cost of living. In September 2026, for example, only 40 per cent of British residents surveyed by YouGov thought Russia posed a major threat to Europe beyond Ukraine.

Garnering political will

Western European governments therefore need to generate political will for improved defence against grey zone warfare. As a first step towards this, governments must invest in the creation and dissemination of awareness campaigns and resources mapping the comprehensive nature of attacks from Russia, Iran, and other malign actors. 

This information needs to be disseminated by verifiable and credible outlets and departments, in anticipation of disinformation already being a demonstrated grey zone tactic. Awareness efforts also must go beyond individual attack attribution and explicitly connect various separate attacks, both domestically and transnationally. Clear messaging enables the public to understand the greater threat posed by grey zone attacks. Governments could also draw upon existing civil society efforts to map grey zone attacks, such as the Ukrainian think-tank Sahaidachnyi Security Center’s sub-threshold warfare tracker, to illustrate the threat to the public. 

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

Increasing public awareness of what is at stake from further grey zone attacks might help persuade the public to support greater defensive measures, including an increase in defence spending to address grey zone vulnerabilities. 

This would help governments to make the case for a two-pronged approach of supplying aid to Ukraine while investing in infrastructure security tailored to specific national and regional needs. Financially, this might also be less expensive overall than exclusively focusing on rearming national militaries for a future conflict.

Without a more forward-looking and unified approach to grey zone attacks, Europe runs the very real risk of offering Russia, Iran and other aggressors the upper hand in any future conflict escalation scenario. The risks of inaction far outweigh any costs of acting now.

The myth of a united Turkic front against Russia, China, and Iran
item.description:
When Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with the leaders of five Central Asian states in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, on October 19, in a format known as 5+1, a sense of contradiction loomed.

Just a few days earlier in Athens, Greece, Rubio had spoken against ancient Persia as an invader and destroyer in a speech purportedly extolling Western civilization. Yet here he was, courting partners in Samarkand, a city that epitomizes the historic Persianate realm, whose inhabitants still predominantly speak Tajik, a variant of Persian. The irony was not lost on Iranian diplomats, who took to social media to troll Rubio over the incongruity.

Rubio was accompanied by over 200 American businessmen at the summit, where he discussed new trade and investment initiatives. The American-Uzbek Business & Investment Council announced 54 deals worth $12 billion as a result of the visit.

As a key hub of the ancient Silk Road, Samarkand is a fitting place to strike trade deals. Rubio spoke of a “fair chance to compete” for American businesses.

There is, however, an influential strand of think tank opinion in Washington that sees Central Asia primarily through the lens of great power competition. In this reading, the U.S. has to assert its influence in the region to counter Russia, Iran and China and empower a “Turkic front” in the region. The neoconservative Hudson Institute is at the vanguard of this effort.

Hudson fellow Ken Moryasu argues that the region is central to the U.S. strategy of containing China, pointing to the region’s overland energy routes, which give Beijing an opportunity to bypass sea lanes where the U.S. has an advantage. His Hudson colleague Michael Doran, a former member of the George W. Bush administration’s National Security Council, is known for his long-standing advocacy for closer ties with Azerbaijan as a gateway to Central Asia and a counterweight to both Russia and Iran.

The advocacy is not limited to Hudson. The American Foreign Policy Council (AFPC), another DC-based think tank, runs a research program focused on the region called Central Asia – Caucasus Initiative (CACI). S. Frederick Starr, Svante Cornell and their co-authors published a strategy paper in 2025 that calls for bringing Azerbaijan into 5+1, appointing a presidential envoy to the region, and securing access to critical minerals for the U.S.

In a separate paper co-authored with Brenda Schaffer, who has a record of undisclosed advocacy for Azerbaijan, Cornell welcomes the “recent rise of Turkish influence in the region” and “the weakening of Iran” as opportunities for Washington. Schaffer also published work for the hawkish Foundation for Defense of Democracies in which she laid the ground for Iran’s fragmentation along ethnic lines, with a particular emphasis on leveraging the Azerbaijani minority against Tehran.

Another Hudson fellow – Luke Coffey – takes the ambition a step further. He calls for cultivating the Organization of Turkic States (OTS). Its membership is not the same as 5+1, but it overlaps with it to a significant extent: its members are four Turkic Central Asian states (Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan with Turkmenistan as an observer) plus Turkey and Azerbaijan, minus the Persian-speaking Tajikistan.

In late October 2026, just after Rubio’s visit, Coffey wrote about the nascent “Turkic century,” calling on Washington to leverage it against Moscow, Tehran and Beijing.

What the Washington hawks tend to overlook, however, is that the Turkic and Central Asian states are far from being a homogenous bloc. These are sovereign states, each with their own domestic and foreign policy priorities that do not align on all occasions, and may, in fact, be in conflict with each other.

The recent spat between Turkey and Azerbaijan is a case in point. The conflict started when Baku imposed fresh restrictions on Islamic headscarves in schools, prompting unusually blunt reactions from members of Turkey’s ruling AKP party, which built its identity, to a large extent, on resisting such restrictions on religious freedom in Turkey.

Joseph Epstein, the director of the Turan Research Center, hosted at the Yorktown University in Washington, DC, defended Baku’s move as an assertion of Azerbaijani sovereignty. The alleged religious influence from Turkey is presented as a threat to that sovereignty – much in the same way the hawks have long treated Iranian influence.

Epstein also happens to be a research fellow at Israel’s Begin-Sadat Center for Strategic Studies, and director of research for Endowment for Middle East Truth (Emet), an explicitly pro-Israeli outfit in Washington. Since pro-Israeli officials and think-tankers increasingly frame Turkey as a “new Iran,” Azerbaijan’s appeal grows not only as Israel’s foothold on Iran’s borders, but also as a check on Turkey’s influence.

One can see in this a new iteration of Israel’s “periphery doctrine”: the original strategy consisted of balancing the hostile Arab core of the Middle East with “moderate” Muslim regimes on its rim, such as the Shah’s Iran and Kemalist Turkey. The fall of the shah and Turkey’s drift from strict Kemalism under the AKP put an end to that arrangement.

Now Iran and Turkey are the ones to be contained and confronted. The Turkic arc consisting of post-Soviet, secular Muslim republics offer Israel, in that reading, a useful counterweight to Turkey and new strategic depth in the Muslim world. Azerbaijan maintains close strategic relations with Israel, and Kazakhstan joined the Abraham Accords last year.

While Turkey, Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan all have strong reasons to cooperate, their differences over Israel and religious freedom will be difficult to overlook. These tensions show how little the common Turkic heritage tells us about their foreign policies.

To complicate the matters further, at the last OTS summit in Ankara, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev floated a role for Russia in the club, potentially as an observer. Astana sees no contradiction in keeping close relations with Turkey, maintaining economic ties with China, and making room for Russia in a Turkic forum. Each relationship serves a purpose in Astana’s multi-vector foreign policy. A one-sided American alignment would upset the balance Tokayev has carefully crafted.

Turkey has options of its own. It can use the OTS to expand links across Eurasia while working with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan through the Mecca Pact to strengthen its position in the Middle East. That framework could eventually provide a way to bring Iran into a wider regional security dialogue. An American strategy to organize the Turkic states against Tehran would narrow Ankara’s room for maneuver and exacerbate its rivalry with Tehran – something the Turkish leaders have so far sought to avoid.

These examples show the absurdity of the idea that the Turkic world and Central Asia act as a geopolitical actor with a common foreign policy and shared strategic outlook. Trying to mold the region into a united front against Russia, China and Iran would ignore the contradictions within that diverse group of countries and risk destroying the balanced policies they have been building.

Washington should resist the reflex to measure the success of its strategy in Central Asia in terms of the regional countries’ alignment with U.S. geopolitical goals. By that measure, every new deal of these states with Moscow, Beijing, or Tehran would become a setback for the U.S. to counter, thus perpetually fueling confrontation. Instead, the U.S. can pursue trade, investment, and transport projects in Central Asia as one of several partners, not necessarily the dominant one.

item.title: The Quad is on life support and Trump is holding the plug
item.description:
Last week the leaders of the Quad (Quadrilateral Security Dialogue )— comprised of Australia, India, Japan, and the United States — met in the Philippines for the first time in two years.

President Donald Trump was in Manila for less than 24 hours with a jam-packed schedule, including his participation in the main event, which was the ASEAN Summit, as well as a bilateral engagement with President Ferdinand Marcos and the Quad summit itself. Perhaps because of this busy itinerary, the Quad was given extremely short shrift, with Trump scheduled to participate for a mere 55 minutes total.

But that was only part of the problem. Since the Quad’s last summit in 2024 during President Joe Biden’s administration, the strategic bloc’s members have grown increasingly frustrated with the lack of formal meetings. India is particularly aggrieved because Trump refused to travel to New Delhi when it hosted the Quad last year.

Indeed, India still believes that it is the rightful next host of the Quad, even though this year is supposed to be Australia’s turn. Trump’s decision to combine the Quad with the ASEAN summit, and to have the Philippines become the first third-party nation to host a Quad summit, has potentially caused otherwise avoidable diplomatic protocol frictions between New Delhi and Canberra.

Moreover, America’s bilateral relationships with each of the Quad members has soured since Trump’s return to the White House. He has strained relations with India by imposing steep tariffs, demanding a trade deal, and resetting ties with Pakistan after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi declined to nominate him for the Nobel Peace Prize. Japan has faced tariffs, demands to dramatically increase defense spending, and criticism for not helping to reopen the Strait of Hormuz as part of his war against Iran. Australia has similarly faced tariffs and pressure to increase defense spending.

Canberra was also kept in the dark about Washington’s decision to counter-blockade Iran, and Trump criticized its refusal to participate in his war.

Meanwhile, during the summit this week, Trump, who prides himself on building personal relationships with foreign leaders, frustrated at least one of them while on stage. Trump’s decision to hold an impromptu press conference, in effect cutting further into the already short Quad time, prompted Modi to ask “Shall we move?” Both Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also stood silently and looked uncomfortable while Trump took questions.

Beyond the awkward atmospherics and limited time spent on Quad matters, the strategic bloc failed to achieve any meaningful policy deliverables. Perhaps the summit’s most significant security announcement concerned the Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration, an initiative designed to improve maritime domain awareness and information sharing. Under the initiative, the Quad members pledged to deploy their P-8 and P-3C maritime patrol aircraft in a joint exercise in 2027.

But the announcement was hardly groundbreaking and in truth is a repackaging of ongoing cooperation. Rather than conducting a standalone Quad exercise, the four nations will integrate their activities into Sea Dragon 2027, an established U.S.-led multinational anti-submarine warfare exercise in which Quad members have previously participated.

Another major announcement was the launch of the Quad Business Leaders’ Forum. In truth, this is also repackaged from previous Quad initiatives. During Biden’s administration, all members in May 2022 agreed to convene a business and investment forum, and the following year, they formally launched the Quad Investors Network (QUIN) to bring together investors and executives from all four countries, leading to the Quad Investment and Technology Dialogue with then-Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo present. In September 2024, at the Wilmington summit, the QUIN highlighted ten strategic investments and partnerships.

Similarly, the Cable Connectivity and Resilience nor Enhanced Quad Cybersecurity Cooperation initiatives simply build upon Biden-era agreements as well. Even the Super Intelligence Accelerator initiative has strong antecedents in the Biden administration, when the Quad established joint research initiatives, worked on safeguards, and pledged funding. By contrast, Trump’s AI program seems more focused on deployment, but does not specifically pledge to do anything new beyond that.

Trump’s decision to fly to Shenzhen immediately after the Quad summit to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping — two authoritarian leaders whose governments stand in opposition to the democratic values underpinning the Quad — further reinforced the perception that he does not necessarily prioritize cooperation with U.S. allies and partners over engagement with America’s rivals. This strikes at the very heart of the Quad and is likely to cause rising anxiety.

While Trump’s participation in the Quad has certainly kept it alive for now, the grouping is on life support. It is abundantly clear that he and his administration are simply rebranding past initiatives and framing them as progress, and they do not take the Quad seriously — particularly when compared to great power relationships. Trump has also made no attempt to repair strained bilateral ties with each of the members, and his personal relationships with their leaders appear to be worsening.

If current trends persist over Trump’s last two years in office, the Quad is likely to become far more symbolic than substantive — an international box-checking exercise rather than a forum for policy achievements — which will only redound to the benefit of Russia and China and diminish the value of the strategic bloc to the rest of the world.

item.title: EU budget blackmail: fund Ukraine or else
item.description:
The European Union is engaged in contentious budget negotiations this week with spending on security and the Ukraine War competing against other priorities, pitting net contributors such as Germany against net recipients like Poland and Hungary.

EU Council president Antonio Costa is trying to hasten adoption of the Multiannual Financial Framework, which runs from 2028 through 2034, because next year’s elections in France, Italy and Poland could bring Euroskeptic leaders to power who may want to cut their countries’ contributions.

This would include the leading presidential candidates in France — Marine Le Pen and Jean Luc Mélenchon — who both call for sharp reductions in France’s contributions.

As the budget drama unfolds, the EU is also moving toward a potential clash over a proposed $49 billion loan to Ukraine, with a final decision to be taken at a meeting of heads of government on November 26-27, in which they will also work toward an agreed draft budget.


Ukraine in the mix: Merz’s gauntlet 


There has long been significant variation among EU member countries in their financial or military support for Ukraine. Support from the Nordic EU member countries is greatest as a share of GDP, but in absolute terms, Germany is the EU’s largest bilateral donor to Ukraine.

Spain and Italy are among the most obvious laggards. The trend in public opinion across the EU is toward greater reluctance to continue funding for Ukraine.

The IMF now estimates that the funding gap for Ukraine’s state budget for the coming year is $76 billion. The EU leadership seeks approval for a new loan of roughly $49 billion, with non-EU supporters of Ukraine to provide the remainder. Under current rules this loan must be approved by all EU member states.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz wrote to council president Antonio Costa on November 10 to say that all EU member countries should financially back the loan to Ukraine. He threatened a German veto of the EU budget if this condition is not met.

Germany is also the largest single contributor to the EU budget, and EU institutions are the largest provider of financial assistance (budget support) to Ukraine. The draft EU budget for 2028-2034 includes generous assistance to Ukraine, but the proposed loan is outside the budget deliberations. The loan is an unanticipated response to Ukraine’s acute financing gap, presumably the consequence of damage to power and other infrastructure inflicted by Russia.

This time it’s different?


At the end of last year, the European Commission tried and failed to get member states’ agreement to provide aid to Ukraine from the frozen Russian reserves held mainly in Belgium’s Euroclear depository. EU members agreed instead to provide a $98 billion loan to Ukraine backed by the EU budget. This loan was intended to meet Ukraine’s financing needs for 2026 and 2027.

The $98 billion loan approved in December 2025 required unanimous approval by member states. To ensure the funds were made available to Ukraine, the EU allowed Hungary, Czechia, and Slovakia to be exempted from any financial obligation in servicing or repaying this loan.

The leaders of Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia and Bulgaria have indicated they are unwilling to back this new EU loan commitment. Merz’s November 10 ultimatum makes clear that Germany will oppose any exemptions or reservations in approval of the proposed loan.

Blowback


In a November 10 press conference with Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico called the German ultimatum “blackmail” and indicated that Slovakia and other EU members can also wield veto power, including over the budget.

In a joint press conference with Merz on November 10, Hungarian Prime Minister Petr Magyar said Hungary did not agree with conditioning the approval of the EU budget on unanimous approval of the proposed EU loan to Ukraine. A November 23 summit of the Visegrad Group (Poland, Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia) prime ministers questioned the usefulness of further negotiations on the EU budget this week, in part because of the controversy around the loan and its relation to the budget.

Consequences


It is obvious in populist circles that EU leadership is speeding this along to avoid any challenges to EU priorities — including support for Ukraine — after the 2027 elections.

The April presidential contest in France could radically tip the balance. Marine Le Pen, leader of the populist right Rassemblement National, has a clear lead in polls. Although Le Pen no longer advocates leaving the EU or the euro, she is outside the EU mainstream on Ukraine/Russia, enlargement, climate, and some defense and security issues. She advocates curbing the power of the European Commission and strengthening the intergovernmental European Council.

Whatever the outcome, Merz’s hardball approach to the Ukraine loan has roiled the already complex budget process. His public ultimatum breaks with the customary tactful and cautious German interactions with EU partners. Typically, Germany has sought to act in concert with like-minded countries and avoided the appearance of throwing its weight around.

Merz’s insistence that Ukraine is a collective European obligation risks aggravating the somewhat submerged discord among EU members over the ever increasing aid to Ukraine. It also slows the adoption of a budget that could limit the potential of populists such as Marine Le Pen to change dramatically the relations between member countries and Brussels.

Merz may have hoped to please the German public by insisting others bear more of the burden of aiding Ukraine, but he did not reckon with other countries’ needs to focus their scarce resources on domestic priorities. The difficult progress toward a multiannual EU budget has been made more complicated.
